guides.title: How to Match Excavator Undercarriage Parts to Your Machine Model
guides.excerpt: A practical 5-step method for procurement teams to match pitch, shoe width, roller diameter and OEM numbers before placing an undercarriage order.
guides.content:
Start with the machine plate, not a photo

Record the model, serial number and country spec. Two machines with the same nominal tonnage can use different pitch, shoe width or roller count. The serial number often identifies brake valves, long-track options and reinforced undercarriage packages.

Measure the five critical dimensions

  • Pitch: distance between pin centers on the chain.
  • Shoe width: measure across the grouser face, not the mounting plate.
  • Roller diameter and flange profile: compare worn and new diameters.
  • Bolt-hole pitch: check center distance and thread size.
  • Seal and oil port: photograph the seal face before ordering a roller.

Use OEM references as a bridge

An OEM number is a useful starting point, but it is not a quality certificate. Ask the supplier to state the material grade, hardness range, seal group and inspection method behind that number.

Standardize inspection before shipment

For rollers, request leak-test records. For chains, request pin hardness and link height. For sprockets, request tooth-root hardness and bolt-hole gauge results. These are faster and more useful than a generic certificate.

Plan mixed-container packing

Ask for pallets grouped by machine or component family. This reduces dock time and makes warranty traceability easier when several models are working on the same site.

guides.title: 5 Failure Signs That Tell You to Replace Track Rollers
guides.excerpt: Identify oil leakage, flat spots, flange wear, vibration and unusual track wander before they destroy chains and sprockets.
guides.content:
1. Oil or grease leakage

A wet roller face or a level drop usually means the floating seal or plug has failed. Continue operating and the internal bearing zone will score rapidly.

2. Flat spots and stepped tread

Flat spots concentrate load on the chain. If the tread is more than 3–5 mm below the flange path on a 20-ton machine, replace before the chain pitch becomes uneven.

3. Flange thinning or sharp edges

Flanges guide the chain. Thin flanges allow lateral movement and accelerate both roller and shoe wear. Measure flange thickness at four positions.

4. New vibration or metal noise

Vibration that changes with travel speed often points to a seized roller, worn bearing zone or failed shaft. Check roller rotation at every service interval.

5. Track wander or misalignment

If one side needs constant adjustment, inspect roller alignment and flange wear together. Replacing only the chain can repeat the failure.

Procurement tip

When replacing more than four rollers, ask for matched hardness and dimensional reports, and inspect each crate on arrival before installation.

guides.title: How to Compare Bucket Teeth Castings Before You Buy
guides.excerpt: Use casting finish, hardness, impact toughness, adapter fit and packing evidence to separate cheap GET from durable parts.
guides.content:
Look beyond surface hardness

A very hard tooth can crack in rock. Ask for both surface hardness and impact toughness. A balanced tooth usually has a hardened working face with a tougher core.

Inspect the adapter pocket

Measure pocket width and pin-hole alignment. A loose fit accelerates pin wear, creates hammering and can damage the adapter long before the tooth is worn out.

Check casting cleanliness

Small porosity on a non-working surface can be acceptable, but cracks, cold shuts or shrinkage near the locking area are reject conditions. Request batch photos or an inspection report.

Test one case before a large order

Install teeth on your most abrasive site, record working hours and failure mode, then compare wear profiles. This is more reliable than price-per-kilogram alone.

Make packing part of the specification

Loose teeth in bulk bags can damage locking collars. Require boxed teeth, separated locks, batch labels and palletized loading.

guides.title: Export Packing and Shipping Guide for Heavy Equipment Parts
guides.excerpt: Plan crate strength, moisture protection, mixed-container labeling, insurance photos and warranty traceability for excavator parts.
guides.content:
Classify parts before packing

Long cutting edges, heavy rollers, sealed chains and precision hydraulic pumps need different protection. Do not accept one generic crate specification for the entire order.

Protect against three transport risks

  • Impact: use internal braces, foam and fixed strapping.
  • Moisture: use VCI film, sealed ports and desiccants for machined surfaces.
  • Handling: mark lifting points and center of gravity on heavy crates.

Make labels useful at the job site

Every pallet should show model, part number, quantity, batch and purchase-order reference. Mixed containers should group by machine or family.

Record loading evidence

Take photos after final packing and after container loading. These support insurance claims and help identify damage caused by transit rather than production.

Prepare documents early

Commercial invoice, packing list, material certificate and HS code should be agreed before booking. This avoids customs delays and allows consignee verification at discharge.
